news.title_zh: 中国新冠后肺炎支原体成为儿童呼吸道感染的主要病原体,两项年研究发现 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A two-year study conducted in Ningbo, Zhejiang province, China, reveals that Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most frequently detected pathogen among pediatric acute respiratory infections, surpassing other viruses like human rhinovirus and human adenovirus. The research, published in BMC Infectious Diseases, analyzed throat swab samples from 34,404 children aged 18 years or younger who presented with respiratory symptoms at the Affiliated Women and Children’s Hospital of Ningbo University. Using multiplex polymerase chain reaction, the team identified 13 common pathogens, finding that 69.14 percent of the samples tested positive for at least one. Mycoplasma pneumoniae accounted for 26.94 percent of the cases, making it the dominant pathogen. The study also notes that 19.85 percent of the samples showed coinfections, with dual infections being the most common. These findings highlight the importance of broad molecular panels in diagnosing respiratory infections and suggest that hospitals can use seasonal trends to anticipate surges in admissions and prepare accordingly. The results emphasize the need for more targeted treatment strategies, as Mycoplasma pneumoniae does not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics commonly used for respiratory complaints.

news.content_title: AdenoVerse Platform Receives FDA Designation for HPV-Associated Cancers
news.content: The FDA granted platform technology designation to the immunotherapeutic platform for use in HPV-positive cancers such as head and neck, cervical, and anal. The FDA has granted platform technology designation to the AdenoVerse immunotherapeutic platform, which is already used in a commercial product, zopapogene imadenovec-drba (Papzimeos), according to a news release from the developer, Precigen. 1 The designation reflects the platform's potential to be applied across a broad range of indications, including human papillomavirus (HPV)–positive malignancies such as head and neck, cervical, anal, vulvar, and vaginal cancers, as well as other diseases that may be targeted by future AdenoVerse-based product candidates. What does platform technology designation mean for AdenoVerse? To qualify for platform technology designation, a platform must already be used in an FDA-approved product, and the available evidence must demonstrate that the platform is well characterized, reproducible, and has the potential to be adaptable across multiple products without compromising quality, manufacturing, or safety. In granting the designation, the FDA determined that AdenoVerse can be applied consistently across multiple products and is reasonably likely to generate meaningful efficiencies in the development, manufacturing, and regulatory review process. The designation creates a pathway to leverage data generated for zopapogene imadenovec-drba in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis to potentially accelerate development of future AdenoVerse programs by using existing manufacturing and preclinical knowledge to support future marketing applications and reduce duplication of development work. It also provides opportunities for early FDA engagement, timely advice through additional interactions with the agency during development, and consideration of prior FDA manufacturing inspections for future applications. “This designation has the potential to accelerate the development of Precigen's broader AdenoVerse portfolio by allowing us to build on the technology established through [zopapogene imadenovec-drba], which was approved by the FDA in August 2025,” stated Helen Sabzevari, PhD, president and chief executive officer of Precigen, in the press release. 1,2 “We expect the near-term impact will be especially meaningful for PRGN-2009 across multiple HPV-associated cancers, including cervical cancer and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. Importantly, the potential extends beyond PRGN-2009 to future AdenoVerse candidates such as those targeting additional cancers and other diseases.” What is in Precigen's AdenoVerse clinical portfolio for HPV-associated cancers? The AdenoVerse portfolio includes a phase 2 study (NCT05996523) of PRGN-2009 in combination with pembrolizumab (Keytruda) in newly diagnosed patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma and a phase 2 study (NCT06157151) of PRGN-2009 in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer. 3,4 What is AdenoVerse and how does it work? AdenoVerse utilizes a library of proprietary adenovectors, including gorilla adenovectors, for the efficient gene delivery of therapeutic effectors, immunomodulators, and vaccine antigens designed to modulate the immune system. 5 The platform's gorilla adenovectors are derived from an adenovirus originally isolated from a healthy gorilla; because they are not recognized by human sera from healthy donors the way common human adenoviral vectors often are, they may be less susceptible to preexisting immunity that can blunt vaccine efficacy. Gorilla adenovectors also allow for repeat administration, are unable to replicate in vivo, which may improve their safety profile, and can deliver a large genetic payload. “We thank the FDA for recognizing the potential of the AdenoVerse platform,” Sabzevari added. 1 “This designation will enable us to leverage prior data and engage with the FDA earlier and more frequently, creating opportunities to reduce duplicative work and bring greater speed, efficiency and predictability to the development of future AdenoVerse therapies.” References Precigen receives FDA platform technology designation for AdenoVerse platform. news.content_original: The FDA granted platform technology designation to the immunotherapeutic platform for use in HPV-positive cancers such as head and neck, cervical, and anal. The FDA has granted platform technology designation to the AdenoVerse immunotherapeutic platform, which is already used in a commercial product, zopapogene imadenovec-drba (Papzimeos), according to a news release from the developer, Precigen. 1 The designation reflects the platform's potential to be applied across a broad range of indications, including human papillomavirus (HPV)–positive malignancies such as head and neck, cervical, anal, vulvar, and vaginal cancers, as well as other diseases that may be targeted by future AdenoVerse-based product candidates. What does platform technology designation mean for AdenoVerse? To qualify for platform technology designation, a platform must already be used in an FDA-approved product, and the available evidence must demonstrate that the platform is well characterized, reproducible, and has the potential to be adaptable across multiple products without compromising quality, manufacturing, or safety. In granting the designation, the FDA determined that AdenoVerse can be applied consistently across multiple products and is reasonably likely to generate meaningful efficiencies in the development, manufacturing, and regulatory review process. The designation creates a pathway to leverage data generated for zopapogene imadenovec-drba in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis to potentially accelerate development of future AdenoVerse programs by using existing manufacturing and preclinical knowledge to support future marketing applications and reduce duplication of development work. It also provides opportunities for early FDA engagement, timely advice through additional interactions with the agency during development, and consideration of prior FDA manufacturing inspections for future applications. “This designation has the potential to accelerate the development of Precigen's broader AdenoVerse portfolio by allowing us to build on the technology established through [zopapogene imadenovec-drba], which was approved by the FDA in August 2025,” stated Helen Sabzevari, PhD, president and chief executive officer of Precigen, in the press release. 1,2 “We expect the near-term impact will be especially meaningful for PRGN-2009 across multiple HPV-associated cancers, including cervical cancer and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. Importantly, the potential extends beyond PRGN-2009 to future AdenoVerse candidates such as those targeting additional cancers and other diseases.” What is in Precigen's AdenoVerse clinical portfolio for HPV-associated cancers? The AdenoVerse portfolio includes a phase 2 study (NCT05996523) of PRGN-2009 in combination with pembrolizumab (Keytruda) in newly diagnosed patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma and a phase 2 study (NCT06157151) of PRGN-2009 in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer. 3,4 What is AdenoVerse and how does it work? AdenoVerse utilizes a library of proprietary adenovectors, including gorilla adenovectors, for the efficient gene delivery of therapeutic effectors, immunomodulators, and vaccine antigens designed to modulate the immune system. 5 The platform's gorilla adenovectors are derived from an adenovirus originally isolated from a healthy gorilla; because they are not recognized by human sera from healthy donors the way common human adenoviral vectors often are, they may be less susceptible to preexisting immunity that can blunt vaccine efficacy. Gorilla adenovectors also allow for repeat administration, are unable to replicate in vivo, which may improve their safety profile, and can deliver a large genetic payload. “We thank the FDA for recognizing the potential of the AdenoVerse platform,” Sabzevari added. 1 “This designation will enable us to leverage prior data and engage with the FDA earlier and more frequently, creating opportunities to reduce duplicative work and bring greater speed, efficiency and predictability to the development of future AdenoVerse therapies.” References Precigen receives FDA platform technology designation for AdenoVerse platform. elements_zh.time: 美国食品药品监督管理局(FDA)于2025年8月授予AdenoVerse免疫治疗平台平台技术资格,如新闻稿所述。该新闻于2026-09-22发布。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 该事件与美国有关,因为FDA是美国机构。该平台用于HPV阳性癌症,如头颈癌、宫颈癌和肛门癌,这些癌症影响人类人群。
elements_zh.event: 美国食品药品监督管理局(FDA)已将AdenoVerse免疫治疗平台授予平台技术资格,用于HPV阳性癌症,包括头颈癌、宫颈癌和肛门癌。该资格基于该平台在广泛适应症中的应用潜力及其在FDA批准产品zopapogene imadenovec-drba中的使用。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 该资格允许利用先前数据并减少未来AdenoVerse疗法的开发重复工作。它还提供了早期FDA参与的机会,可能加速HPV相关癌症疗法的开发,如宫颈癌和口腔鳞状细胞癌。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: FDA已确定AdenoVerse可以在多种产品中一致应用,并且合理可能在开发、制造和监管审查中产生有意义的效率提升。该平台的潜力基于其在FDA批准产品中的使用及其良好的特性描述。

news.content_zh: 美国食品药品监督管理局(FDA)已将AdenoVerse免疫治疗平台授予平台技术资格,该平台已被用于商业产品zopapogene imadenovec-drba(Papzimeos)。该资格认可了该平台在广泛HPV阳性恶性肿瘤中的应用潜力,包括头颈癌、宫颈癌、肛门癌、外阴癌和阴道癌,以及其他疾病。FDA认为AdenoVerse可以在多种产品中一致应用,并且合理可能在开发、制造和监管审查中产生有意义的效率提升。该资格使Precigen能够利用先前数据,减少未来AdenoVerse疗法的开发重复工作,特别是PRGN-2009与pembrolizumab联合用于HPV相关癌症的疗法。该平台的gorilla腺病毒载体来源于健康大猩猩,可能对预先存在的免疫力具有较低的敏感性,从而允许重复给药并提高安全性。该新闻于2026年9月22日发布,该资格于2025年8月授予。

supplementary_news.content: Abstract Pulmonary infections are common in hospitals. Radiological imaging is crucial for rapid diagnosis, revealing infection patterns and distinguishing them from non-infectious conditions. This review highlights key radiological features that aid in diagnosing pulmonary infections and identifying causative organisms to guide therapy. Bacterial pneumonias may show lobar, bronchial, or interstitial patterns, characterised by lobar consolidation, bronchial wall thickening, and alveolar septal thickening, respectively. Viral infections typically present a multifocal ground-glass pattern. An airway-centric pattern, with “tree-in-bud” opacification and bronchial wall thickening, may also occur, often coexisting with bacterial infections, which can complicate diagnosis. Fungal infections, particularly dangerous for immunocompromised individuals, can be suggested by CT imaging features such as the halo, reverse halo, and air-crescent signs. Given the complexities and limitations of timely diagnosing pulmonary infections, accurately interpreting radiological findings is vital. Enhancing our ability to use imaging effectively enables healthcare professionals to make better prescribing decisions, aiming for more targeted therapies and improved patient outcomes. Introduction & Background Lower respiratory infections remain the deadliest communicable disease group and were the fifth leading cause of death worldwide in 2021 [1]. Although they affect people of all ages, they cause disproportionate morbidity and mortality in the elderly and immunocompromised, whose numbers are growing [2]. Complex patients presenting with difficult-to-treat underlying pathogens create a diagnostic challenge that necessitates precise and timely identification to avoid incorrect or delayed treatment. Fungal infections, in particular, pose a significant challenge due to their rapid progression and high fatality rate, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Similarly, viral infections can present with multifocal patterns that complicate differentiation from bacterial infections, with both types often present concurrently, further clouding the diagnostic picture [3]. Although empirical treatment targeting the most likely organism is often started immediately, the risks associated with broad-spectrum therapies (e.g., antimicrobial resistance) and the high mortality associated with misdiagnosis warrant pursuing a specific diagnosis. Thus, the importance of detailed imaging cannot be overstated [4]. Early imaging with chest radiographs and computed tomography (CT) is an important component of diagnostic evaluation. It is more readily accessible than invasive procedures such as biopsies and bronchoalveolar lavage and provides more rapid diagnosis compared with culture samples. Imaging thus complements these and other diagnostic techniques. Effective imaging can help distinguish between different types of infection and suggest the likely causative agent, helping to inform appropriate and effective treatment. However, as with all diagnostic tools, radiological tests do have limits and do not have perfect specificity or sensitivity in lung infection diagnosis [5]. This narrative, pictorial review is based on a non-systematic search of PubMed and Google Scholar (using terms such as “pulmonary infection,” “pneumonia,” “CT,” “chest radiograph,” and organism-specific terms) together with standard radiology reference texts. Representative and illustrative sources were selected at the authors' discretion, and no formal systematic search, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis was undertaken. All figures are original clinical images from the authors' own archives at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, fully anonymised, and are reproduced with appropriate local approval; no images are reproduced from third-party sources, and no reproduction permissions were, therefore, required. Table 1 details key terms and signs referred to within this review. Review Bacterial infections Bacterial pneumonia is common and results from bacterial colonisation and a buildup of inflammatory products within the lung. Bacterial lung infection can demonstrate a number of patterns on imaging (as respectively demonstrated in Figure 1) [5]. Lobar Pneumonia Inflammatory exudates collect within the alveoli, and the infection spreads to adjacent segments through interalveolar pores of Kohn, leading to confluent areas of consolidation, confined to a single segment or lobe. On CT, there might be adjacent ground-glass opacities (GGOs) caused by partial alveolar filling. Infection can spread between lobes via incomplete major fissures [5]. Bronchopneumonia The infection leads to bronchial wall thickening, mucus plugging, and peribronchiolar inflammation. This appears as centrilobular nodules, tree-in-bud pattern, and peribronchiolar consolidation with a patchy non-segmental distribution [5]. Interstitial Pneumonia Inflammatory cells infiltrate the alveolar septa and interstitial tissues, leading to septal thickening, nodules, and areas of GGO on imaging [5]. As many pathogens can be responsible for pneumonia with more than one pattern, pneumonias are categorised as community-acquired, hospital-acquired, or aspiration pneumonia, as this helps narrow down the likely causative organisms and guide empirical therapy [6]. Community-Acquired Pneumonia As the name suggests, community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) refers to infections acquired outside of healthcare facilities, by definition (or becoming apparent within the first 48 hours of admission, beyond which it is termed hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP)). Designation of infection as CAP is based upon this “pre-hospital acquisition” definition and is not specific to a particular pathogen; similarly, the pathogens commonly involved in CAP are not specific to it. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila are the most common causative organisms in CAP [6, 7]. Streptococcus pneumoniae has been identified in 33-50% of predominantly hospitalised adults in developed countries with community-acquired pneumonia in whom a microbial aetiology could be established [8]. It usually demonstrates a lobar pattern with a preference for the lower lobes, but multi-lobe involvement is also common [9]. Some evidence suggests parapneumonic effusions are becoming more common in the UK, associated with serotypes 1 and 3 despite vaccination programmes [10]. Mild lymph node enlargement may be evident [11]. Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia can occur in children and older patients, and particularly in smokers and those with chronic lung disease or immunocompromised status, and is seen in both CAP and HAP (discussed later in the article). The nasopharynx is often colonised by this organism, which can cause pneumonia when translocated to the lower respiratory tract [12]. There is usually a peripheral predominance, with GGO, centrilobular nodules and consolidation all being common radiological features [13]. Staphylococcal pneumonia is a relatively rare cause of CAP, implicated in around 5% of cases, but is commonly the causative organism in HAPs and can also complicate viral pneumonias. The prevalence of Staphylococcus aureus, for example, in HAP has been reported as over 18% in Italian populations, and is acquired through haematogenous spread or aspiration. Imaging features include pulmonary consolidation, abscess, and cavitation and can have associated complex effusions [14, 15]. Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and imaging features reflect different stages of infection (Figure 2) [16]. Primary TB, where a patient is infected for the first time, manifests as (1) dense consolidation anywhere in the lung, particularly the mid- and lower zones in adults; (2) lymphadenopathy, particularly in children and typically right unilateral, and is often a differentiator when there are otherwise non-specific appearances of bacterial pneumonia; (3) miliary disease, which is rarer and usually seen in immunocompromised, infant, or elderly patients and where tiny randomly distributed nodules are present throughout the lungs; (4) pleural effusion, which is usually a delayed manifestation and essentially never seen in infants [16]. Post-primary TB occurs in patients who have had previous exposure and experience either re-infection or re-activation of infection; features are similar to those of primary TB but with the classic upper zone predilection, often with bilaterality, generally a lack of lymph node enlargement (although previously calcified nodes may be evident) and cavitation from exuberant immune response. Endobronchial spread is seen as tree-in-bud opacities on CT. Mucoid impaction can cause lobar collapse, as can bronchial stenosis, a fibrotic sequela of infection. Fibrotic scarring also causes parenchymal scarring, particularly at the apices, and traction bronchiectasis [16]. Non-tuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary infection is a separate entity, presenting as bronchiectasis and bronchial wall thickening and, on CT, GGO and tree-in-bud opacities, which can also cause suspicion of TB [16]. Mycoplasma spp. pneumonia usually affects young people. It is clinically characterised by dry cough, fever, and general fatigue. It can have a variable radiological appearance but most commonly demonstrates a bronchopneumonia pattern with bronchial wall thickening, centrilobular nodules and peribronchial consolidation. However, more widespread consolidation can also be seen. The radiographic appearance of Chlamydia spp. pneumonia is similar to that of Mycoplasma spp. and the two infections sometimes coexist [17]. Legionella spp. pneumonia is acquired by the inhalation of droplets of contaminated water, most frequently from water systems which become colonised by this pathogen [18]. Patients present with cough, dyspnoea, diarrhoea, headache, and myalgia. On CT, sharply marginated peribronchial consolidations within GGO are characteristic of Legionella spp. pneumonia [19]. Pulmonary nocardiosis predominantly affects immunocompromised patients. Nocardia asteroides is the most commonly implicated pathogen. Imaging demonstrates multifocal consolidation with abscess formation (Figure 3C). Cavitation develops in up to a third of cases, and centrilobular nodularity and peripheral GGO may be evident. In chronic infection, bronchiectasis, pleural thickening, and collections may develop [20]. Melioidosis, caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, is a disease of the tropics, being especially endemic in northern Thailand and Queensland, Australia. Pulmonary infection is most common, usually manifesting as upper lobe infiltrates, with or without thin-walled cavitation, although diffuse infiltrates may be seen acutely. Lymph node enlargement is rare, which can help differentiate from post-primary TB [21]. Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia Nosocomial or HAP is defined as a pneumonia occurring beyond 48 hours after admission and up to 48 hours after discharge from hospital. The infection is often caused by multiple organisms, including Gram-negative bacilli (Enterobacterales, including E. coli, and the aerobic non-fermenting Pseudomonas aeruginosa), and Gram-positive cocci (S. aureus and S. pneumoniae) [22]. The infections are more frequent and severe in intensive care (ICU) patients. Mechanical ventilation is a major risk factor since it can facilitate bacterial dissemination, and sputum clearance is reduced due to an impaired cough. However, HAP can also occur in non-ventilated ICU patients [22]. The radiographic pattern of HAP is variable. Most commonly, patients demonstrate unilateral or bilateral consolidation, but nodules and GGO may also be seen. Differentiating HAP from other pulmonary abnormalities frequently seen in ICU patients such as pulmonary infarction, oedema or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) can be challenging [23]. Pulmonary infiltrates due to both pulmonary oedema and ARDS tend to be bilateral, symmetrical and with an anterior-to-posterior gradient. Focal asymmetrical consolidation favours infection over oedema [23]. Aspiration Pneumonia Inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the respiratory tract can lead to aspiration pneumonia. The aspirated contents may consist of bacterial flora, gastric acid or food debris, which can respectively lead to bacterial pneumonia (usually anaerobic), chemical pneumonitis or granulomatous reaction. Imaging findings include airway plugging with aspirated contents and associated atelectasis, centrilobular nodules with surrounding GGO, and bilateral consolidation in the dependent areas of the lungs (Figure 3E) [24]. Complications Immunocompromised patients are more susceptible to complications from bacterial pneumonia, which can occur with both CAP and HAP infections. Parapneumonic pleural effusions (Figure 3A) may develop in up to 60% of hospitalised pneumonia patients. While in most cases these are reactive and resolve with antibiotic therapy, in around 5% of cases, they become complicated and progress to empyema [25]. Lobar enlargement occurs with an extensive exudative process. While the finding was initially seen as specific for Klebsiella spp. pneumonia, other suppurative processes, including tuberculosis, can also cause lobar enlargement (Figure 3D) [26]. Cavitation can occur in immunocompetent patients, for example with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus; right upper lobe cavitation is shown in Figure 3B. Cavitation can also be seen in Aspergillus spp. infections in immunocompromised patients [26]. As discussed above, cavitation is also a feature of post-primary TB [16, 26]. Table 2 summarises the imaging appearances of bacterial pulmonary infection. Viral infections There is significant overlap in the imaging appearances of viral infections, and it is thus not possible to make a specific aetiological diagnosis of a viral pneumonia on imaging alone. However, viral infections are a frequent occurrence in immunocompromised patients, with cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, measles and adenovirus being common causative organisms [27]. Imaging patterns can be variable and affected by the immune status of the host, with more progressive and diffuse imaging abnormalities being more common in immunocompromised patients. It is thus important to consider history and examination findings, with insidious onset, disproportionately high tachycardia and tachypnoea compared to pyrexia being indicators of viral infection over bacterial. Moreover, co-infection with bacteria is common. Nonetheless, recognising a viral pneumonia can prevent the presumption of bacterial infection and allow for more judicious use of antibiotics [27]. Viral infections predominantly demonstrate a multifocal GGO pattern and tend to be more diffusely distributed than bacterial infections. Airway-centric abnormalities may be encountered, with tree-in-bud opacification and bronchial wall thickening. Cavitation, lymphadenopathy, or pleural effusions are not common findings [28]. We will now outline the typical imaging features of common and important viral pneumonias. Most influenza viruses often cause mild to moderate seasonal upper respiratory tract infections in immunocompetent patients. In immunocompromised patients, those with chronic diseases, the elderly, or infants, severe complications such as haemorrhagic bronchitis or pneumonia may occur. In early stages of the disease, tracheobronchitis or neutrophilic bronchopneumonia patterns may be demonstrated. In later stages, this progresses to diffuse alveolar damage with intra-alveolar oedema and haemorrhage [29]. On imaging, this manifests as bilateral patchy GGO/consolidation and ill-defined small nodules, particularly in the lower lobes (Figure 4A). Pleural effusions are rare. Development of lobar consolidation indicates secondary bacterial pneumonia [30]. Human parainfluenza virus (HPIV) infection demonstrates a variety of clinical manifestations, which include conjunctivitis, otitis media, croup, pharyngitis, and pneumonia. It is the second most common virus in patients receiving care in intensive treatment units and is a common cause of death in patients with haematological malignancies [31]. CT shows multiple areas of patchy GGO and consolidation and bronchial wall thickening. Centrilobular nodules may be present. The features are difficult to differentiate from bacterial pneumonia, and bacterial co-infection is a common occurrence [32]. Adenovirus accounts for approximately 5-10% of paediatric respiratory tract infections [33, 34]. Immunocompetent patients present with mild upper respiratory symptoms which resolve within two weeks. In immunocompromised patients, the infection is more severe and can be a fatal condition [34]. On imaging, adenovirus pneumonia may resemble bacterial pneumonia with multifocal GGO and patchy consolidations in a segmental or lobar distribution. Changes may be unilateral or bilateral. Hyperinflation and atelectasis are frequently seen in infant and child populations. Long-term sequelae of adenovirus pneumonia include bronchiectasis, bronchiolitis obliterans, and unilateral hyperlucent lung (Swyer-James-Macleod) syndrome (Figure 4D) [28]. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection is predominantly seen in immunocompromised patients and can lead to necrotising tracheobronchitis, interstitial pneumonitis, or necrotising pneumonia. Patients with pulmonary infection may be pyrexial and have a productive cough, shortness of breath, and upper airway obstruction due to the formation of pseudomembranes resulting from tracheal ulcers [28]. On imaging, HSV pneumonia predominantly demonstrates multifocal segmental or subsegmental GGO with focal areas of consolidation (Figure 4C). Pleural effusion is common [35].
